title: Knowledge Check 6: Lessons 26-29
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 26-29 of the hermes-consultant series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Per the lesson, what is the actual job of a contract or statement of work?
options: To satisfy lawyers and satisfy an administrative requirement
To replace a fragile shared memory of a verbal agreement with something both sides can inspect, so neither side can drift from it quietly
To set the highest possible fixed fee for the work
To list only the deliverables while leaving the exclusions unwritten
questions.explanation: The lesson says the contract's job is not legal posturing but to make the agreement explicit enough that neither side can drift from it quietly, because early drift is cheap and late drift is a betrayal.

questions.question: Which is the biggest single source of scope creep, according to the lesson?
options: A client acting in bad faith to get free work
A retainer engagement that names its included work
Ambiguity: when the work is not defined, no change is out of scope because there is no scope to be out of
A clear change process that makes every change visible and priced
questions.explanation: The lesson states that scope creep is a failure of the handshake, not of the client's character, and that ambiguity is the biggest source because a vague definition invites every addition to be considered in scope.

questions.question: In the worked example, when the client asks the consultant to add weekly summaries, what does the lesson recommend doing?
options: Say yes because the request is small and friendly
Say no because all new work is forbidden under the contract
Absorb the addition silently as part of the existing scope to keep the client happy
Use the change process: name it as new scope, scope it, price it, and add it as a separate bounded piece of work with its own acceptance test
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the consultant says yes through the change process, making the summary a separate bounded deliverable with its own written scope, which keeps the original boundary intact and the client un-surprised.

questions.question: Per the lesson on building a repeatable delivery framework, what is the central focus?
options: A tutorial on marketing agent products to new clients
Building the machine that delivers the next dozen clean engagements without reinventing the process each time
A review of unrelated project-management software
A summary of payroll policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is about turning a one-off engagement into a repeatable delivery framework so you stop paying the same learning cost on every project.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance on a delivery framework?
options: A framework is complete with just the phases and templates, since checklists slow down delivery
A framework that lives in a document nobody opens is as useless as a process that lives in your head
The playbook should stay in your head so it is not transferable to competitors
A framework should be rewritten from scratch after every engagement
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that a framework must be enforced with checklists and gates, not just captured in a document, or it is decoration.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support about capturing a delivery framework?
options: A retrospective should produce one or two targeted improvements, not a full rewrite, after each engagement
Talent scales better than a playbook because instinct survives fatigue
The failure mode of a solo consultant is incompetence, not skipping checkpoints
Templates alone guarantee consistent quality without needing checklists
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches the continuous-improvement loop: run a retrospective and make targeted changes, keeping the framework a living tool rather than a museum piece.

questions.question: Per the lesson about upselling and expanding, what is the central focus?
options: Turning a single win into a lasting client relationship by recognizing the natural next engagement and offering it honestly
A tutorial on writing more aggressive sales proposals
A review of unrelated customer-support tools
A summary of lead-generation tactics for cold outreach
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on treating each win as the opening of a longer relationship, reading the delivery record for the adjacent need, and offering expansion honestly rather than hard-selling.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance on when to raise the next engagement?
options: Wait until the contract ends and the client is no longer using the system
Ask at the moment the delivered work proves itself, while the client is actively feeling its value
Ask only after receiving a referral from a third party
Let the client bring up expansion unprompted, since asking risks looking greedy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that people expand a relationship when they feel its value most sharply, so the expansion checkpoint belongs at the mid-point and close while value is fresh, not at the cold end of the contract.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support about the most reliable form of expansion?
options: The larger one-off project, because it generates a bigger single payment
The hard sell, because the client needs to be convinced to spend
The standing deliverable on a schedule, because it converts a project into recurring value the client does not have to prompt for
Cold outreach, because new clients are the only source of growth
questions.explanation: The lesson argues the standing deliverable is the most reliable expansion because it keeps the account alive and converts a project into recurring revenue the client gets without asking, which is easier to say yes to than a new project.

questions.question: In client communication, what is the difference between status and progress, and why does keeping them separate matter?
options: Status is the distance traveled toward done and progress is how the work feels, so they never conflict
Status is where the work actually is right now against the plan, while progress is the distance traveled toward done, and the risk is reporting progress while hiding a stalled status
Status is what the client asks about and progress is what you report, so progress always takes precedence
Status and progress are the same thing reported from two different calendars
questions.explanation: The lesson defines status as where the work actually is right now against the plan, and progress as the distance traveled toward done. You can truthfully report progress while a blocker has the engagement parked, which is the polite version of a lie.

questions.question: Why does a status update have to reflect reality, and what is the single core move this lesson teaches?
options: A client can see your running process, so an update is only a courtesy and does not need to be checkable
An update should sound confident so the client does not lose faith, even when a detail is unverified
A client cannot see your work, so the update is their only window, and the core move is to verify before you claim, pairing every assertive verb with its proof
An update should summarize your best feelings about the day rather than the state of the work
questions.explanation: The lesson says a client cannot see your running process, test runs, or the reason a task is late, so everything they believe comes through your updates. The core move is verify before claim and pair every assertive verb with proof.

questions.question: When you surface a problem early, what are the four things a well-formed update should name, and why does the blast radius matter?
options: The client, the budget, the deadline, and the apology, because managing the relationship beats managing the problem

The observed failure, the investigation, the blast radius, and the verification target, because naming the blast radius turns a scary unknown into a bounded, manageable fact the client can plan around
The fix, the timeline, the cost, and the owner, because the client should only hear about a problem once it is solved
The date discovered, the date reported, the date resolved, and the date billed, because paperwork keeps everyone honest
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches the four-part update: the observed failure, the investigation, the blast radius, and the verification target. Naming the blast radius specifically turns a vague worry into a bounded fact a client can plan around instead of fear.
